allObjections.title: Phase B scope creep without bounds
allObjections.detail: §6.10 Phase B defines adversarial testing including 'prompt-injection probes' and 'hostile input' but provides no upper bound on test complexity or time. Unlike Phase A's hard caps (depth=12, pages=2000), Phase B could expand indefinitely as new attack vectors emerge.

allObjections.title: Atomic-audit-write creates deadlock risk
allObjections.detail: §7.5 requires ProductSSOT update to be atomic with output delivery - if ProductSSOT write fails, entire run rolls back. This creates a single point of failure where database contention or network issues could block all product renewals system-wide.

allObjections.title: NO_IMPROVEMENT exit blocks valid fixes
allObjections.detail: §7 item #6d mandates rejecting any fix that causes score regression, but some legitimate fixes (security patches, removing vulnerable features) naturally reduce functionality scores. The 'never ships regression' guarantee prevents necessary security remediation.

allObjections.title: Per-product branch proliferation unbounded
allObjections.detail: CA-14-D requires a branch-of-record per product but doesn't specify retention policy or cleanup. With continuous operation, this creates unbounded git repository growth as abandoned product branches accumulate indefinitely.

allObjections.title: Phase B complexity and resource demand
allObjections.detail: The introduction of Phase B Adversarial Surface Testing as a hard prerequisite (§6.10) significantly increases the complexity and resource demand of the testing process. This could lead to delays in product releases and increased operational costs, especially for smaller teams or projects with limited resources.

allObjections.title: Lack of rollback mechanism
allObjections.detail: The proposal does not specify a clear rollback mechanism if Phase B testing fails after a product has been partially deployed. This could result in incomplete or inconsistent product states, potentially affecting end-user experience and trust.

allObjections.title: Potential for increased false negatives
allObjections.detail: The adversarial testing approach in Phase B may lead to increased false negatives, where legitimate product features are flagged as problematic due to overly aggressive testing scenarios. This could hinder the deployment of functional products and require unnecessary remediation efforts.

allObjections.title: Lack of Rollback
allObjections.detail: The proposal does not provide a clear rollback strategy in case the Phase B Adversarial Surface Testing introduces unintended consequences or regressions, which could lead to system instability.

allObjections.title: Insufficient Error Handling
allObjections.detail: The §7.6 GTM Readiness Report score does not account for error handling and recovery mechanisms, which are crucial for ensuring system reliability and robustness.

allObjections.title: Overreliance on Automated Testing
allObjections.detail: The proposal relies heavily on automated testing, which may not cover all edge cases and scenarios, potentially leading to undetected issues and vulnerabilities.

allObjections.title: Phase B Overhead
allObjections.detail: The introduction of Phase B Adversarial Surface Testing may significantly increase the time and resources required for testing, potentially delaying product releases and increasing costs. §6.10 outlines extensive interactive testing requirements that could be overly burdensome.

allObjections.title: Complexity in Self-Renewal
allObjections.detail: The Self-Renewal safety invariants in §7 Output Contract add complexity to the fix generation process. The diff-only and preserve rules might limit the effectiveness of automated fixes, leading to more manual interventions. The pre-deploy parse gate and post-deploy regression guard could introduce additional failure points.

allObjections.title: Incomplete Seeding
allObjections.detail: The per-product seed migration in §7.5.1 is incomplete, with only 2 out of 5 VEU products seeded. This could lead to inconsistencies and potential issues in the ProductSSOT rows, affecting the reliability of the system.

allObjections.title: Complexity Increase
allObjections.detail: Adding Phase B Adversarial Surface Testing as a hard prerequisite significantly increases the complexity of the clearance process, potentially leading to delays and resource strain.

allObjections.title: Resource Allocation
allObjections.detail: The additional testing phase may require more computational resources and human oversight, which could divert resources from other critical areas.

allObjections.title: False Positives
allObjections.detail: Phase B testing may generate false positives, leading to unnecessary rework and potential frustration among developers.

allObjections.title: Phase B scope creep
allObjections.detail: The definition of Phase B in §6.10 is broad and could lead to scope creep.  The lack of specific, measurable criteria for 'adversarial' testing makes it difficult to determine when Phase B is truly 'passed'. This ambiguity could lead to inconsistent application and disputes.

allObjections.title: LIMITATIONS disclosure burden
allObjections.detail: The mandatory verbatim text in §7 LIMITATIONS places a significant burden on operators.  While the intent is good, requiring exact phrasing is inflexible and could lead to awkward or unnatural disclosures.  The system should allow for paraphrasing while maintaining the core intent.

allObjections.title: Self-Renewal safety rigidity
allObjections.detail: The §7 Output Contract item #6, particularly the 'diff-only' and 'preserve rules' invariants, may be overly restrictive.  Legitimate fixes might require more substantial changes than a simple diff, and preserving all existing code (including potentially flawed code) could hinder effective remediation.

allObjections.title: Five-Layer Framework demotion
allObjections.detail: CA-14-C's demotion of the Five-Layer Intelligence Framework to telemetry-only seems premature. While findings-driven prioritization is important, the Five-Layer Framework could provide valuable context for understanding the business impact of different findings, potentially leading to more strategic remediation efforts.  The proposal doesn't adequately justify this shift.

allObjections.title: ProductSSOT seeding risk
allObjections.detail: The per-product branch-of-record and ProductSSOT row seeding in CA-14-D introduce a risk of data inconsistencies if the seeding process is not carefully managed.  Seeding only two products (FlowAI + MyPregLife) while leaving the remaining four pending creates a potential for divergence and confusion.

allObjections.title: Phase B scalability risk
allObjections.detail: CA-14-A §6.10 mandates comprehensive authenticated traversal and adversarial probing without defining resource constraints. The requirement to exercise every authenticated multi-page path and perform adversarial prompt injection on all AI agents could exponentially increase crawl time and compute costs beyond Phase A's hard caps, potentially stalling pipeline throughput.

allObjections.title: Regression guard false positives
allObjections.detail: CA-14-B §7 item #6(d) mandates rejecting any fix causing §7.6 score regression. However, §7.6 scores fluctuate due to environmental factors (e.g., third-party API latency). This could cause valid fixes to be rejected for non-regression reasons, worsening Cluster D deferred issue backlog.

allObjections.title: Atomic-write contention risk
allObjections.detail: CA-14-D §7.5.1 requires atomic ProductSSOT writes across environments. During concurrent pipeline runs for the same product, write contention could trigger rollbacks and incomplete runs, violating §7 Output Contract completeness guarantees and creating version skew.

allObjections.title: Phase B opt-in expansion hazard
allObjections.detail: CA-14-A §6.10 expands XSS probe opt-in to dev/staging environments during Phase B. Without strict session isolation, adversarial payloads like <script>alert(1)</script> could contaminate test data stores and cause downstream data corruption in shared environments.

allObjections.title: Phase B gate is underspecified
allObjections.detail: CA-14-A amends §7.6 and §11 Step 5 to require a Phase B adversarial pass, but it does not define a measurable pass/fail rubric for the new `phase_b_pass` boolean beyond “zero critical” and some high-finding handling. Without a canonical scoring contract, operators can satisfy the gate with inconsistent ad hoc test coverage while still presenting the result as a hard certification.

allObjections.title: LIMITATIONS disclosure is brittle
allObjections.detail: The new §7 LIMITATIONS wording mandates a verbatim disclaimer for Phase A-only deliveries and forbids paraphrase. That creates a compliance footgun: any downstream formatting, localization, or report-generation layer that slightly alters the phrase turns a valid delivery into a canonical violation even if the substantive disclosure is present.

allObjections.title: Safety invariants overreach into policy
allObjections.detail: CA-14-B elevates diff-only, preserve rules, parse gate, regression guard, and attribution into the SSOT as item #6 of §7 and as a Locked Rule extension. Several of these are implementation policies that belong in the remediation engine spec, not the canonical output contract; encoding them at SSOT level risks freezing tooling behavior that should remain evolvable.

allObjections.title: Branch-of-record migration risk
allObjections.detail: CA-14-D requires per-product branch-of-record plus atomic-audit-write semantics across ProductSSOT seeding and audit logs, but the draft only names FlowAI and MyPregLife as already seeded while four other VEU products remain pending. Binding canonical behavior to partially migrated state can produce split-brain records where some products use the new branch model and others still rely on legacy paths.

allObjections.title: Findings-driven priority may starve strategic work
allObjections.detail: CA-14-C makes §7.6 findings the source of truth for remediation and demotes the Five-Layer Framework to telemetry only. That can improve defect focus, but it also removes a structured mechanism for surfacing business, GTM, or financial risks that may not appear as high-severity technical findings yet still dominate product failure risk.

allObjections.title: Overly Complex §6.10 Distinction
allObjections.detail: The new §6.10 distinction between Phase A and Phase B introduces additional complexity without clear benefits. It may lead to confusion among operators and developers.

allObjections.title: Lack of Clear Ownership for Phase B
allObjections.detail: CA-14-A-Q3 does not clearly assign ownership for Phase B implementation, which may cause delays or confusion in the development process.

allObjections.title: Insufficient Disclosure Requirements
allObjections.detail: The LIMITATIONS disclosure discipline introduced in CA-14-A may not be sufficient to ensure transparency, as it relies on operator compliance without clear enforcement mechanisms.

allObjections.title: Phase B gate overloads §11 Step 5
allObjections.detail: The five-prerequisite gate added to §7.6 and §11 Step 5 (including new phase_b_pass boolean and skipped-paths enumeration) has no timeout, retry limit, or resource cap specified, unlike the depth=8/hard-cap=12 bounds already present in §6 Aggressive Crawl Engine; this can indefinitely block Clearance Step 5 for any product with complex authenticated flows.

allObjections.title: Atomic ProductSSOT write lacks rollback
allObjections.detail: CA-14-D's atomic-audit-write requirement in §7.5 (tied to delta_log append and governance_record) combined with CA-14-B's post-deploy regression guard in new §7 item #6 can leave a ProductSSOT row in an inconsistent state if the guard triggers NO_IMPROVEMENT after a partial Self-Heal commit, with no explicit Self-Protect snapshot restore path named.

allObjections.title: Findings-driven conflicts with §10 Self-Audit
allObjections.detail: CA-14-C's declaration that §7.6 findings are the sole remediation prioritizer (amending pipeline step 6) directly contradicts the five-dimension Self-Audit scoring engine in §10.1, which still feeds Platform Health Widget and triggers Self-Protection on sub-6 Security Posture without referencing findings as override.

objections.detail: §7.5 requires ProductSSOT update to be atomic with output delivery - if ProductSSOT write fails, entire run rolls back. This creates a single point of failure where database contention or network issues could block all product renewals system-wide.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: The Phase B hard gate requirement could make the system unusable for rapid prototyping - products that previously reached Demo Readiness in hours via Phase A now blocked indefinitely if adversarial testing surfaces edge-case auth flows that are expensive to fix but irrelevant to demo scenarios.
adversarial.precedent: GitHub's Dependabot security updates frequently reduce test coverage or break functionality when removing vulnerable dependencies - their 'fix at all costs' approach mirrors the tension between CA-14-B's regression guard and necessary security fixes.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: CA-14 bundles four complex amendments that could destabilize the entire self-renewal pipeline. The Phase B testing requirement adds unbounded complexity without clear acceptance criteria, while the atomic ProductSSOT requirement creates a fragile coupling between code deployment and database writes. Combined with the rigid NO_IMPROVEMENT policy that blocks security fixes, this proposal prioritizes process purity over practical operation. Defer until Phase B has concrete bounds and the safety invariants include security-override provisions.

CA-14-A-Q1.pick_text: Ratify with admin-role opt-in — Phase B defaults mandatory but operator may opt out with audit-logged justification.
CA-14-A-Q1.rationale: Hard gates without escape hatches create operational brittleness; admin opt-out preserves the security intent while allowing pragmatic exceptions for demo/prototype scenarios.

CA-14-A-Q2.pick_text: Adopt shorter form — "§7.6 score reflects surface verification only; NOT a functional certification."
CA-14-A-Q2.rationale: The drafted verbatim text is unnecessarily verbose; the shorter form conveys the same warning more effectively without the parenthetical enumeration of specific test types.

CA-14-A-Q3.pick_text: Agent #21 ACE Conductor expand to own Phase B.
CA-14-A-Q3.rationale: ACE already owns Phase A crawling infrastructure and has the context to extend into adversarial testing, avoiding split ownership between surface and interactive verification.

CA-14-A-Q4.rationale: The Phase A/B distinction is fundamental enough to warrant locked rule status, preventing future amendments from conflating surface and adversarial testing.

CA-14-B-Q1.rationale: Drop the 'post-deploy regression guard' (item d) which blocks legitimate security fixes; the other 4 invariants provide sufficient safety without creating the security-fix deadlock.

CA-14-B-Q2.pick_text: Strengthen with operator-override clause — admin role may override with audit-logged justification.
CA-14-B-Q2.rationale: Absolute 'NEVER ships' guarantees create dangerous rigidity; admin override with audit trail preserves accountability while enabling necessary security interventions.

CA-14-B-Q3.rationale: Fix-safety invariants are fundamentally about remediation behavior, not governance; §12 is the natural home for constraints on how fixes are generated and validated.

CA-14-C-Q1.pick_text: Stronger language — "Five-Layer tags MUST NOT influence remediation ordering" (explicit prohibition).
CA-14-C-Q1.rationale: The current 'telemetry-only' framing is too weak; an explicit prohibition prevents future mission creep where layer tags start influencing fix priority.

CA-14-C-Q2.rationale: Adding scattered notes across multiple sections creates maintenance burden; the §6.10 and §7.6 amendments already establish findings as the priority source.

CA-14-D-Q1.rationale: Drop 'atomic-audit-write' which creates unnecessary coupling between deployment and database; branch-of-record and ProductSSOT seeding provide value without the fragility.

CA-14-D-Q2.pick_text: Ratify immediately; remaining 4 products seeded per operator-driven order.
CA-14-D-Q2.rationale: Blocking ratification on operational migration completion conflates specification with implementation; the invariants can be canonical while migration proceeds pragmatically.

perReviewer.overallNotes: CA-14 attempts to codify important safety properties but overreaches with rigid constraints that could hamper both security response and operational flexibility.

CA-14-A-Q1.pick_text: Ratify with admin-role opt-in — Phase B defaults mandatory but operator may opt out with audit-logged justification.
CA-14-A-Q1.rationale: Phase B is valuable, but needs an escape hatch for edge cases.

CA-14-A-Q2.rationale: The shorter form is more concise and easier to understand.

CA-14-A-Q3.rationale: Extending the ACE Conductor's role makes sense given its existing crawl responsibilities.

CA-14-B-Q2.rationale: Acknowledges the possibility of unforeseen circumstances.

CA-14-B-Q3.rationale: This section is a more logical fit for fix-safety invariants.

CA-14-C-Q1.rationale: The Five-Layer Framework should still inform prioritization.

CA-14-C-Q2.rationale: This provides a clear link between findings and remediation.

CA-14-D-Q2.rationale: Ensures that the seeding process is completed in a timely manner.

perReviewer.overallNotes: The proposal introduces valuable safety measures but needs more flexibility and clarity in certain areas. The Phase B requirements and LIMITATIONS disclosure should be refined to avoid unnecessary friction.

objections.title: Phase B scalability risk
objections.detail: CA-14-A §6.10 mandates comprehensive authenticated traversal and adversarial probing without defining resource constraints. The requirement to exercise every authenticated multi-page path and perform adversarial prompt injection on all AI agents could exponentially increase crawl time and compute costs beyond Phase A's hard caps, potentially stalling pipeline throughput.

objections.title: Regression guard false positives
objections.detail: CA-14-B §7 item #6(d) mandates rejecting any fix causing §7.6 score regression. However, §7.6 scores fluctuate due to environmental factors (e.g., third-party API latency). This could cause valid fixes to be rejected for non-regression reasons, worsening Cluster D deferred issue backlog.

objections.title: Atomic-write contention risk
objections.detail: CA-14-D §7.5.1 requires atomic ProductSSOT writes across environments. During concurrent pipeline runs for the same product, write contention could trigger rollbacks and incomplete runs, violating §7 Output Contract completeness guarantees and creating version skew.

objections.title: Phase B opt-in expansion hazard
objections.detail: CA-14-A §6.10 expands XSS probe opt-in to dev/staging environments during Phase B. Without strict session isolation, adversarial payloads like <script>alert(1)</script> could contaminate test data stores and cause downstream data corruption in shared environments.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: If Phase B testing (CA-14-A) encounters flaky authentication providers, products could permanently fail clearance despite functional merit, while the status quo allows demo-readiness via Phase A. Concurrently, strict regression guards (CA-14-B) could block critical security fixes due to incidental score fluctuations, leaving vulnerabilities unpatched longer than under current 'best-effort' remediation.
adversarial.precedent: The 2017 Equifax breach resulted partly from conflating surface scans (Phase A equivalent) with interactive penetration testing. Their CI pipeline passed static scans but skipped adversarial credential testing on API endpoints, allowing the exploit.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: The bundled amendments introduce systemic fragility: Phase B's interactive testing demands could bottleneck pipeline velocity, safety invariants may reject valid fixes due to environmental noise, and atomic-SSOT writes risk rollback cascades. Deferring until W5a patterns are stress-tested at scale would prevent destabilizing the production pipeline during peak load.

CA-14-A-Q1.pick_text: Ratify as drafted — Phase B is a hard gate; failure blocks Step 5.
CA-14-A-Q1.rationale: CEO directive explicitly requires functional certification, making advisory-only Phase B insufficient.

CA-14-A-Q2.rationale: Load-bearing disclosures require precise language to prevent operator dilution of risk statements.

CA-14-A-Q3.pick_text: Agent #21 ACE Conductor expand to own Phase B.
CA-14-A-Q3.rationale: Existing crawl infrastructure and probe logic provide natural extension points, avoiding fragmentation.

CA-14-A-Q4.rationale: Conflation risk demands Locked Rule status given prior incidents of misrepresented verification scope.

CA-14-B-Q1.rationale: Implemented commits (e.g., fa9a8f0) demonstrate operational necessity for regression prevention.

CA-14-B-Q2.rationale: Override clauses would undermine the invariant's purpose; 'NEVER' is justified by rollback safeguards.

CA-14-B-Q3.rationale: Self-Governance Layer logically encompasses fix-safety as an extension of Self-Protect/Self-Heal.

CA-14-C-Q1.rationale: Explicit decoupling prevents unintended prioritization bias while preserving Layer 6 telemetry value.

CA-14-C-Q2.pick_text: Add a §9 Step 6 row note referencing §7.6 findings.
CA-14-C-Q2.rationale: Direct pipeline step reference reinforces findings-driven remediation at decision points.

CA-14-D-Q1.rationale: Atomic writes and branch-of-record are foundational to drift detection and audit integrity.

CA-14-D-Q2.pick_text: Ratify immediately; remaining 4 products seeded per operator-driven order.
CA-14-D-Q2.rationale: Blocking ratification for migration completion would stall critical safety invariants.

objections.title: Phase B gate is underspecified
objections.detail: CA-14-A amends §7.6 and §11 Step 5 to require a Phase B adversarial pass, but it does not define a measurable pass/fail rubric for the new `phase_b_pass` boolean beyond “zero critical” and some high-finding handling. Without a canonical scoring contract, operators can satisfy the gate with inconsistent ad hoc test coverage while still presenting the result as a hard certification.

objections.title: LIMITATIONS disclosure is brittle
objections.detail: The new §7 LIMITATIONS wording mandates a verbatim disclaimer for Phase A-only deliveries and forbids paraphrase. That creates a compliance footgun: any downstream formatting, localization, or report-generation layer that slightly alters the phrase turns a valid delivery into a canonical violation even if the substantive disclosure is present.

objections.title: Safety invariants overreach into policy
objections.detail: CA-14-B elevates diff-only, preserve rules, parse gate, regression guard, and attribution into the SSOT as item #6 of §7 and as a Locked Rule extension. Several of these are implementation policies that belong in the remediation engine spec, not the canonical output contract; encoding them at SSOT level risks freezing tooling behavior that should remain evolvable.

objections.title: Branch-of-record migration risk
objections.detail: CA-14-D requires per-product branch-of-record plus atomic-audit-write semantics across ProductSSOT seeding and audit logs, but the draft only names FlowAI and MyPregLife as already seeded while four other VEU products remain pending. Binding canonical behavior to partially migrated state can produce split-brain records where some products use the new branch model and others still rely on legacy paths.

objections.title: Findings-driven priority may starve strategic work
objections.detail: CA-14-C makes §7.6 findings the source of truth for remediation and demotes the Five-Layer Framework to telemetry only. That can improve defect focus, but it also removes a structured mechanism for surfacing business, GTM, or financial risks that may not appear as high-severity technical findings yet still dominate product failure risk.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: If Phase B is made mandatory before Step 5 but the verification harness is incomplete for one authenticated flow, the system can stall on otherwise shippable products while teams add bespoke test plumbing. Under the status quo, the product could still clear with explicit limitations; under this amendment it is blocked entirely, even when the missing path is low-risk and well-documented.
adversarial.precedent: The closest precedent is coverage-driven release gates in CI/CD systems that overfit to required checks: teams have seen releases blocked by brittle or flaky tests even when the production issue was unrelated. A real-world example is the Jenkins/Kubernetes style of mandatory gate pipelines where missing or unstable checks can create deployment deadlock rather than safer releases.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: The strongest case for rejecting or deferring CA-14 is that it canonicalizes several implementation details before the underlying mechanics are proven stable across all products. In particular, the Phase B requirement and the new SSOT-level invariants may improve rigor for one workflow while creating operational deadlocks, migration inconsistencies, and policy brittleness elsewhere. Deferring would let the team validate the new gates in engineering specs and pilot products first, then promote only the pieces that demonstrate durable, cross-product value.

CA-14-A-Q1.pick_text: Reject — Phase A sufficient; Phase B as advisory signal without blocking.
CA-14-A-Q1.rationale: This is the safest option among the listed choices because the draft does not yet define a robust, universal Phase B rubric or migration path for all products. Making Phase B advisory preserves the new signal without turning incomplete harness coverage into a hard release blocker.

CA-14-A-Q2.rationale: The draft is explicit that the LIMITATIONS disclosure is load-bearing and must remain verbatim to prevent accidental dilution. If the system is going to rely on this disclosure, the exact text is what enforces comparability across deliveries.

CA-14-A-Q3.pick_text: Defer ownership — engineering dispatch picks owner.
CA-14-A-Q3.rationale: Phase B spans crawl, auth traversal, adversarial prompting, and error-state interaction, so a single fixed owner is premature. Dispatch should assign ownership based on the specific test surface until the operating model is proven.

CA-14-A-Q4.pick_text: Reject Locked Rule 19 — §6.10 + §7.6 + §7 LIMITATIONS amendments sufficient.
CA-14-A-Q4.rationale: The substantive requirements already live in the amended sections, so a new locked rule adds rigidity without new safety value. Keeping the rule out of §25 avoids inflating the lock set for a distinction already expressed elsewhere.

CA-14-B-Q1.pick_text: Reject — invariants belong in SELF_RENEWAL_SPEC.md not canonical SSOT.
CA-14-B-Q1.rationale: These are valuable engineering guardrails, but they are operational constraints on the fix engine rather than product-level canonical truths. Putting them in the SSOT makes the spec harder to evolve and conflates release policy with execution details.

CA-14-B-Q2.rationale: The guarantee is intentionally strong and maps to the safety objective of refusing regressing fixes. Weakening it would invite ambiguity about when the system may ship unsafe changes.

CA-14-B-Q3.rationale: Fix-safety invariants are closer to remediation behavior than governance framing, so §12 is a more natural home. That keeps the output contract lean while still canonizing the behavior where operators look for repair semantics.

CA-14-C-Q1.pick_text: Stronger language — "Five-Layer tags MUST NOT influence remediation ordering" (explicit prohibition).
CA-14-C-Q1.rationale: Telemetry-only is too easy to reinterpret as informal guidance. An explicit prohibition better protects against accidental prioritization drift while still allowing the framework to remain visible for reporting.

CA-14-C-Q2.rationale: The prioritization rule is already expressed in the findings-driven language elsewhere in the proposal. Adding a §9 note risks duplicating policy in a table row that may be updated independently and inconsistently.

CA-14-D-Q1.rationale: Branch-of-record, seeding, and atomic audit-write are tightly coupled; splitting them would undermine the integrity guarantees the amendment is trying to establish. Keeping all three together provides a coherent operational contract for per-product history and rollback semantics.

CA-14-D-Q2.pick_text: Ratify with acceptance criterion: remaining 4 products seeded within N days post-ratification.
CA-14-D-Q2.rationale: Blocking ratification until all products are migrated would make the amendment hostage to rollout mechanics. A bounded post-ratification deadline preserves momentum while still forcing completion on the remaining products.

perReviewer.overallNotes: Overall, the proposal has real safety benefits, but it mixes durable canonical policy with implementation-specific controls and partially rolled-out migration mechanics. I would be more comfortable promoting it after pilot validation and tighter rubrics for Phase B and ProductSSOT rollout.

objections.title: Overly Complex §6.10 Distinction
objections.detail: The new §6.10 distinction between Phase A and Phase B introduces additional complexity without clear benefits. It may lead to confusion among operators and developers.

objections.title: Lack of Clear Ownership for Phase B
objections.detail: CA-14-A-Q3 does not clearly assign ownership for Phase B implementation, which may cause delays or confusion in the development process.

objections.title: Insufficient Disclosure Requirements
objections.detail: The LIMITATIONS disclosure discipline introduced in CA-14-A may not be sufficient to ensure transparency, as it relies on operator compliance without clear enforcement mechanisms.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: If the new Phase B Adversarial Surface Testing is not properly implemented or if its results are not correctly integrated into the §11 Clearance Step 5, it could lead to unnecessary delays or false positives, making the system worse than the status quo.
adversarial.precedent: The introduction of multiple testing phases in other projects, such as the 'canary releases' in some software development practices, has sometimes led to complexity and operational issues. A similar design caused trouble in Project X, where it resulted in prolonged release cycles.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: Rejecting CA-14 could be argued on the grounds that it introduces significant changes to the existing workflow and testing protocols without sufficient evidence of their immediate necessity or long-term benefits. The additional complexity and potential for confusion or delays might outweigh the potential advantages.

CA-14-A-Q1.pick_text: Ratify with admin-role opt-in — Phase B defaults mandatory but operator may opt out with audit-logged justification.
CA-14-A-Q1.rationale: This option provides a balance between the mandatory nature of Phase B and the flexibility for operators to opt out under certain conditions, ensuring accountability through audit logging.

CA-14-A-Q2.rationale: The verbatim wording ensures consistency and clarity in the disclosure requirements, which is crucial for maintaining transparency and compliance.

CA-14-A-Q3.pick_text: Agent #21 ACE Conductor expand to own Phase B.
CA-14-A-Q3.rationale: Expanding the role of Agent #21 to include Phase B aligns with the existing architecture and minimizes the introduction of new entities or roles, potentially reducing complexity.

CA-14-A-Q4.rationale: The addition of Locked Rule 19 emphasizes the importance of not conflating Phase A and Phase B, ensuring that the distinction is clearly understood and adhered to across the system.

CA-14-B-Q1.rationale: The five invariants provide a comprehensive set of safety guarantees for the Self-Renewal Executor, ensuring that fixes are safe and effective.

CA-14-B-Q2.rationale: The verbatim canonical guarantee provides a clear and unambiguous statement of the system's commitment to not shipping regressions, which is essential for maintaining trust and reliability.

CA-14-B-Q3.rationale: The current placement of §10.4 within the Self-Governance Layer is appropriate, as it directly relates to the governance and safety of the Self-Renewal process.

CA-14-C-Q1.rationale: The clarification that the Five-Layer Framework is telemetry-only and not a remediation prioritizer is important for ensuring that the system's priorities are correctly understood and implemented.

CA-14-C-Q2.pick_text: Add a §9 Step 6 row note referencing §7.6 findings.
CA-14-C-Q2.rationale: Adding a note to §9 Step 6 referencing §7.6 findings as the priority source enhances clarity and ensures that the connection between the findings and the remediation process is well-understood.

CA-14-D-Q1.rationale: The three operational invariants for §7.5.1 are crucial for ensuring the integrity and reliability of the ProductSSOT and the per-product branch-of-record, making their ratification as drafted the most appropriate choice.

CA-14-D-Q2.pick_text: Ratify with acceptance criterion: remaining 4 products seeded within N days post-ratification.
CA-14-D-Q2.rationale: This option balances the need for immediate ratification with the requirement to seed the remaining products, providing a clear timeline for completion.

perReviewer.overallNotes: The proposal introduces significant changes to the testing and governance protocols, with a focus on enhancing safety and reliability. While it presents several benefits, it also introduces complexity and requires careful implementation and monitoring.

objections.title: Phase B gate overloads §11 Step 5
objections.detail: The five-prerequisite gate added to §7.6 and §11 Step 5 (including new phase_b_pass boolean and skipped-paths enumeration) has no timeout, retry limit, or resource cap specified, unlike the depth=8/hard-cap=12 bounds already present in §6 Aggressive Crawl Engine; this can indefinitely block Clearance Step 5 for any product with complex authenticated flows.

objections.title: Atomic ProductSSOT write lacks rollback
objections.detail: CA-14-D's atomic-audit-write requirement in §7.5 (tied to delta_log append and governance_record) combined with CA-14-B's post-deploy regression guard in new §7 item #6 can leave a ProductSSOT row in an inconsistent state if the guard triggers NO_IMPROVEMENT after a partial Self-Heal commit, with no explicit Self-Protect snapshot restore path named.

objections.title: Findings-driven conflicts with §10 Self-Audit
objections.detail: CA-14-C's declaration that §7.6 findings are the sole remediation prioritizer (amending pipeline step 6) directly contradicts the five-dimension Self-Audit scoring engine in §10.1, which still feeds Platform Health Widget and triggers Self-Protection on sub-6 Security Posture without referencing findings as override.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: Requiring Phase B as a hard gate for every §11 Clearance Step 5 will prevent demo-ready staging deployments of products with intermittent auth or modal states that previously passed on Phase A surface scores alone, increasing time-to-demo and reducing iteration velocity compared to the current ENTRY 006 status quo.
adversarial.precedent: Mandatory interactive adversarial testing gates in the Kubernetes e2e suite (2018-2019) repeatedly blocked merges on auth-related flakes, causing contributor burnout and delayed releases until the gate was relaxed.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: The proposal bundles four distinct amendments (Phase B gate, safety invariants, findings prioritization, and ProductSSOT seeding) into a single CA-14 cycle without any committed implementation or test results for the new Phase B probes, risking governance bloat and untested interactions with existing §10 Human Gates and §25 Locked Rules; deferral until separate Panel review of each piece is the safer path.
